extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, constitutional scholars, and comparative government analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical exposition of what makes a constitution successful, contrasting 'dignified' and 'efficient' constitutional parts and comparing Cabinet (parliamentary) and Presidential systems with attention to authority, habit, legislative-executive relations, and political education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gain then use authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Every constitution must first GAIN authority, and then USE authority; it must first win the loyalty and confidence of mankind, and then employ that homage in the work of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority is a two-stage requirement: a constitution must secure popular reverence (to 'gain' authority) before it can effectively apply power (to 'use' authority). Failure to secure initial loyalty undermines any subsequent exercise of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignified parts vs Efficient parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions have two parts: the DIGNIFIED parts (those which excite and preserve the reverence of the population) and the EFFICIENT parts (those by which it, in fact, works and rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both parts are necessary: dignified parts attract motive power and reverence, while efficient parts employ that power. They are not strictly separable in practice but are functionally distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of dignified parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The dignified parts of Government are those which bring it force—which attract its motive power; they are preliminaries and prerequisites of all work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dignified institutions may not do the 'business' of government as efficiently as simpler mechanisms, but they supply the vital strength via habit, reverence, and theatrical appeal that mobilize popular support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of efficient parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The efficient parts only employ that power; they are the mechanisms that actually do political work and execute policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficient institutions should be simple, modern, and closely fitted to the practical needs of administration; their simplicity aids effective action even when the dignified exterior is complex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of tradition and habit
rubrics_metrics.description: The dull traditional habit of mankind guides most men's actions; yesterday's institutions are by far the best for to-day because they are ready, influential, and easy to get obeyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design must account for human habit and inherited reverence — newly created institutions lack the ingrained authority of longstanding ones and are harder to make effective quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for theatrical/dignified elements to mobilize masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatrical elements (mystic, brilliant, occult, or specious aspects) appeal to the masses and excite easy reverence; these elements will be adjusted to the lowest orders who are uninterested in plain utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A constitution that relies only on plainly useful mechanisms will fail to mobilize broad public support; symbolic and ceremonious features are politically necessary to bind diverse and less-cultured populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transplantability: efficient core vs august exterior
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple efficient part of the English Constitution may, mutatis mutandis, be transplanted to many various countries, but its august outside is narrowly confined to nations with analogous history and political materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exporting constitutional elements, expect the practical machinery (efficient parts) to adapt more easily than the dignified, historically rooted symbols and ceremonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and essential character of the Cabinet
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cabinet is a committee of the legislative body selected to be the executive body—a combining committee that joins the legislative part of the State to the executive part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential characteristics: chosen by the legislature; composed of persons agreeable to and trusted by the legislature; functions as executive though originating in the legislature. Historical accidents (e.g., crown's role) are incidental, not essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cabinet's unique powers (fusion, dissolution, secrecy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Cabinet, though a committee of the legislative assembly, is a committee which can dissolve the assembly which appointed it; it has a suspensive veto and often conducts its business in secret without official minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These powers (collective responsibility, ability to threaten resignation/dissolution, secrecy of deliberation) make the Cabinet an effective executive able to compel legislation and appeal to the electorate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary (Cabinet) advantage for variable administration
rubrics_metrics.description: In a civilised age administration requires the continued aid of legislation; the Cabinet system (fusion) enables the executive to obtain concurrence of the legislature in changing and varied legislation (taxation, budgets, social measures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because administrative needs and expenditures vary, close legislative-executive connection avoids chronic quarrels between tax-imposers and tax-requirers and prevents responsibility-diffusion that hampers effective governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential separation weakens aggregate government
rubrics_metrics.description: The division of the legislature and the executive in Presidential governments weakens the whole aggregate force of Government, and therefore weakens both halves; it produces quarrels and hampered action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation can lead to legislative-executive deadlocks, inability to pass complex budgets, and difficulties assigning responsibility; in crises the lack of dissolution/resignation mechanisms frustrates coordinated response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative debates as civic education and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Cabinet government ensures debates which can produce a change of Government (a 'catastrophe' at the end), and these decisive debates educate the nation, forcing it to form opinions and making public life matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When debates have real consequences (ability to change government), they are attended, influential, and instructive; in systems where debates lack effect (Presidential), public political engagement and the quality of press debate suffer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of presidential-era press and public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Presidential systems the press and public have less motive to form sustained, high-quality opinions because they cannot effect change between elections; newspapers and public debate tend to be less substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional structure shapes incentives for media and civic engagement; designers should consider how institutional responsiveness fosters a cultured public sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merits of secondary election via a fit legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: A Cabinet elected by a legislature (a secondary election) is often the best mode of selecting executives because a good Parliament is a fit electoral body: continuous, close to political life, and representative of varied interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the legislature is competent and representative, its choice of executive yields better, continuously accountable leadership than a large, unskilled national constituency or a manipulated primary electorate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of ministers' membership on separation vs fusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether ministers are members of the legislature is decisive: inclusion tends toward fusion (Cabinet government), exclusion helps maintain separation (Presidential systems); the American exclusion aimed to keep branches distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional rules about ministerial membership materially affect the balance of powers and the tendency toward either collaborative or antagonistic inter-branch relations.
